newsitem.title: USA: Regional growth firm, no signs of slowing - KC Fed.
newsitem.headline: Regional growth firm, no signs of slowing - KC Fed.

text.p: Growth in the 10th U.S. economic district is healthy across the board, with tight labor markets, but less evidence of mounting wage pressures than in recent months, a Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City official said.

"We sense the economy in our district continues to operate at a healthy pace and we see no signs that we would see any substantial slowing in the region's growth," Kansas City Fed vice president and economist Mark Drabenstott told Reuters.
The Kansas City Fed is responsible for the nation's 10th economic district encompassing Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Wyoming, northern New Mexico and western Missouri.
Drabenstott said the regional economy has performed well overall, particularly in manufacturing, service and agriculture.
"We have a manufacturing base that is performing very well and we're also seeing considerable strength out of the service and non-manufacturing segments of the economy," he said.
Drabenstott said the district's agricultural sector was expected to put in its best performance in three years in 1997.
He highlighted the wheat and cattle industries, which have rebounded from recent losses.

"One of the things we were concerned about last year is that we had a very bad wheat crop in our district ... and we also had subtantial losses in the cattle industry. (But) both of those have turned around," he said.

"We are looking at a very good wheat crop this year and the cattle industry is now earning profits. The agriculture in our district is probably going to have the best year it's had in the past three this year," the Fed economist added.
He did not provide specific numbers or details for his forecasts in the agriculture sector.
Drabenstott said the district's labor markets have been very tight. "One indicator of that is growth in jobs over the past year. We've been outpacing the nation by a considerable margin," he said.
Through January 1997, the 10th district chalked up 2.8 percent growth in total employment compared to 2.2 percent for the nation, the economist said.
Drabenstott added that regional employment growth had leveled off by mid-1996, but, "As we moved through the fourth quarter and early 1997, we've seen (job) growth pick up here in the 10th district."
The Kansas City Fed economist said, however, he has not seen an increase in wage pressures in the region.

"As we have noticed in our Beige Book reports, we have had some spot reports of wage pressures. But in our most recent surveys, we suggested there has been actually somewhat less evidence of wage pressures than in recent months," he said.
He did not comment on issues related to monetary policy.

The Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, which includes representatives of all 12 regional Fed banks, last raised its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent at the March 25 meeting.
At the time, the Fed issued a statement saying the action was taken "in light of persistent strength in demand, which is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances."
It added that "the slight firming of monetary conditions is viewed as a prudent step that affords greater assurance of prolonging the current economic expansion."
